newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary's farmers hit hard times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary's farmers hit hard times.

text.p: Cash-strapped Hungarian farmers say their struggle with murky ownership rights and outdated machinery can at best keep them around break-even level, despite expectations of a bumper crop this year.
Hungary's agriculture is mired in a structural crisis which is likely to loom large in forthcoming accession talks with the European Union.

"We have four (former) East German combine harvesters 13 to 15 years old," said Janos Varnyu, president of the small Keve cooperative set on a sandy patch of plain in the village of Rackeve, about 100 km (60 miles) south of Budapest.
The cooperative works 1,550 hectares (3,830 acres) of leased farmland, of which, Varnyu says, the property rights for 500 hectares are unclear.
"We pay an annual lease of 25 kg of milling wheat per gold crown...but in some cases we pay to people who don't actually own the land," Varnyu said.

Hungary -- a country which once prided itself on its productive agriculture -- has a 100-year-old system of farmland valuation under which one hectare is worth an average 25 gold crowns. According to the biggest farmers' union MOSZ, that is currently equivalent in market value to between 50,000 forints ($264) and 100,000 forints ($528).
POST-COMMUNIST LAND REFORM LEFT MAZE OF SMALL FARMS
The current vague ownership rights date back to the communist era.

After elections in 1990, mammoth state-owned cooperatives were disbanded and some farmland was distributed to former cooperative members and other plots granted as compensation to those whose properties were confiscated by the communist government in the 1950s and 1960s.
Self-styled private cooperatives sprung up on the remnants of bigger state-owned farms, in many cases led by the same people who ran them in the communist age.
The accountant of one such cooperative, Kiskun MTSZ, said the company farms 1,100 hectares (2,990 acres) leased from 1,100 different owners.
The typical lease length is five years but most owners either do not understand or disregard lease contracts, several sources said.
"Although I lease lands for five years, in many cases the owners sell it to someone else regardless of our contract," said Karoly Jozsa, from the village of Kiskunhalas in the same region.
LIQUIDITY PROBLEMS

Jozsa runs a small cooperative and also works as an individual farmer and said that his single biggest problem was liquidity, with the unclear property rights making it almost impossible to get loans.
"Four years ago we had to close our cattle farm as we did not have the money to perform vital maintenance," Jozsa said.
Varnyu said that, when his company took over the formerly state-owned cooperative worth some 100 million forints in 1992, it had debts of 33 million forints, which have since worsened.
"This year we plan turnover of 130 million (forints) and we have debts amounting to 70 million," he said.
COSTLY EQUIPMENT, LOW SELLING PRICES, NARROW MARGINS
He added that since 1992 the cooperative could only make 28 million forints worth of investments, buying a 22 million forint dessicator and a six million forint Russian "Don" harvester.
"We could not afford a Klaas or a John Deere and this one almost does the same job," Varnyu said.
He said that, although Keve has plenty of storage capacity, it cannot afford to wait for favourable grain prices but has to sell at whatever the price is at harvest time.

On the Budapest Commodity Exchange, August milling wheat prices are currently under 20,000 forints per tonne and falling, compared with some 24,000 forints for the August 1996 maturity this time last year.
The accountant of another cooperative said that, although they do not have liquidity problems, their seven percent profit margin hardly allows them more than essential maintenance.
Geza Kaali said their best harvester from the former communist East Germany is seven years old but some of their tractors are 20 years old.
"Since 1990 the price of agricultural machinery has risen tenfold," he said.
Cash shortages also prevent some farms from using the required amount of fertilisers and, according to MOSZ, weed control was only performed on 60 percent of the country's cropland this year.
The reduction in livestock since 1990 has resulted in a shortage of manure, a vital ingredient for improving soil composition.
LIGHT AT THE END OF THE TUNNEL
However, one trader said problems of central Hungary's farmers represent the middle ground between two extremes.

"In the western parts of the country, farmers are in a much better situation," said Istvan Grebats, managing director of grains trading company Termin. "But there are other places in the east where things are even worse".

Amendments to a farmland bill, expected to be passed in September, could solve some of the financing problems, as cooperatives would be able to lease land for up to 40 years, thus allowing them to plan for longer periods.
The bill would also allow companies, including foreign-owned firms, to buy farmland which they could mortgage afterwards.
The same bill would also have the long-term effect of concentrating ownership in fewer hands, Grebats said.
"Undoubtedly, land concentration is the future," he said.

The bill could trigger the rebirth of large farms, as economic reason would be likely to convince farmers that big is beautiful, despite bad memories of huge state-owned farms. ($ = 189.2 Hungarian Forints)
